terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs the query in that file against a fresh copy of the practice's database and prints the rows.

tasks.title: Find the owners with no email
tasks.description:
Winnie will phone every owner the practice has no email for.

In `queries/1-no-email.sql`, return three columns from `owners`, in this order:

- `first_name`
- `last_name`
- `phone`

Only owners whose `email` is missing (`NULL`). Any order of rows. Check compares the columns and the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Run a query with the three columns and `email`, and find the owners with `NULL`.
Write a condition that keeps only those owners.
Take `email` out of the columns again and run the file.
hints: If your query runs and returns no rows, read the lesson's part "What NULL is" again.
A missing value is never equal to anything, not even to `NULL`. It has a test of its own.
The condition is `WHERE email IS NULL`.

tasks.title: List the visits with notes
tasks.description:
Ifan wants to read back through the visits he and Mabel wrote notes on.

In `queries/2-visit-notes.sql`, return three columns from `visits`, in this order:

- `visit_date`
- `vet`
- `notes`

Only visits whose `notes` are not missing. Any order of rows. Check compares the columns and the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Run a query with the three columns and look at the `notes`.
Keep only the rows where a note was written.
Run it: no `NULL` should be left in the notes column.
hints: This is the opposite of task 1.
`IS NULL` has an opposite that keeps only the rows where a value was recorded.
The condition is `WHERE notes IS NOT NULL`.

tasks.title: Find the dogs that are not Labradors
tasks.description:
Ifan wants every dog that is not a Labrador, and he was clear that a dog whose breed nobody knows counts too.

In `queries/3-not-labradors.sql`, return two columns from `animals`, in this order:

- `name`
- `breed`

Only dogs, and of those only the ones whose `breed` is not `Labrador`, including dogs whose `breed` is missing. Any order of rows. Check compares the columns and the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Run a query that keeps the dogs and look at their breeds, `NULL` included.
Leave out the Labradors and run it again. Count the dogs with no breed: are they still there?
Bring the dogs with no breed back in.
Make sure no cat or rabbit came in with them.
hints: Count the dogs with no breed in your result. The lesson's part "Conditions skip empty cells quietly" says where they went.
Keep a dog when its breed is something else, or when its breed is missing. That is an `OR`, next to an `AND` about the species.
The condition has the shape `WHERE species = 'dog' AND (breed <> '...' OR breed IS NULL)`.

tasks.title: Make one contact list
tasks.description:
Winnie wants one way to reach every owner on a single list.

In `queries/4-contact-list.sql`, return three columns from `owners`, in this order:

- `first_name`
- `last_name`
- `contact`: the owner's `email`, or their `phone` when the email is missing

Every owner, in any order of rows. Check compares the columns and the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Run a query with the names, `email` and `phone`, and see which owners have no email.
Replace the two columns with one that falls back from the email to the phone.
Name it, and run the file: no `NULL` should be left in it.
hints: Every owner stays in the list, so this needs no `WHERE`. The work happens in a column.
`COALESCE` gives back the first of its values that is not `NULL`. The order you list them in matters.
The column has the shape `COALESCE(first_choice, fallback) AS contact`.
